1,658 unowned Brokers sitting inside the Anvil AMM just had NFTs dropped directly into their wallets

Now anyone can go treasure hunting

But I think there’s a much bigger flywheel forming here

Every StonkBroker has a base relationship with 666,666 $STONKBROKER through Anvil

If the secondary NFT floor falls far enough below the value of those tokens after fees, arbitrageurs can:

Buy the floor Broker → swap it into Anvil → receive $STONKBROKER → sell the ERC20

That helps bind the NFT and token markets together

Now add ERC-6551:

Two Brokers can have the same base conversion value while one happens to contain a Yardkeeper, Chain Mancer or Card Wall NFT

So traders now have another reason to inspect individual Brokers, snipe mispriced wallets and trade the floor

And every additional Anvil trade generates fees which feed back into the Clock In reward engine

Special Projects drop assets → Brokers become more valuable/unequal → treasure hunting + arbitrage increases → more trading volume → more fees → larger reward distributions → more value accrues to Brokers

The NFT is becoming the container for an entire economic flywheel

So the trade is effectively:

1. Find a loaded Broker in Anvil
Broker contains, say, a Chain Mancer worth X

2. Snipe it with 666,666 $STONKBROKER + the Anvil fee

3. You now own the Broker → therefore control its ERC-6551 wallet

4. Transfer the Chain Mancer / other transferable assets from the Broker wallet to your normal wallet

5. Sell those assets

6. Send the now-empty Broker back into Anvil

7. Receive 666,666 $STONKBROKER back

So economically you have round-tripped the principal and extracted the contents of the wallet.

There is a big catch: fees determine whether it’s profitable. Anvil documents a 10% ETH trade fee for a normal swap and 15% for sniping a specific Broker. Because treasure hunting probably requires sniping the exact loaded Broker, you’re likely looking at a 15% fee getting in plus the normal swap fee getting back out, plus gas/slippage

TL;DR: Difficulty in entering the game is inversely correlated with difficulty in playing the game.

The game’s easiest to play when no one wants to play it, in its infancy, but that in itself makes it hard: having conviction in the game when no one believes in it.

The game becomes harder as more players enter, but loses its reward multiplier as it gets easier in terms of conviction: it’s no longer asymmetric.

I.e. entering the game when it’s hard (playing the game when it’s easy) > playing the game when it’s hard (entering the game when it’s easy)

The next phase of RWAs is making onchain assets more productive.

One emerging model uses covered-call vaults to generate option premium on tokenized gold. Deposited gold backs calls auctioned to market makers, with the premium paid upfront to the vault. At expiry, the position settles and the strategy can repeat during the next epoch.

The strategy is already established in traditional markets, where gold option-income products manage hundreds of millions of dollars.

That income comes with a tradeoff. Depositors keep their gold plus the premium when gold finishes below the strike. If gold finishes above the strike, they still keep the premium but miss out on any gains beyond that price.

This is an early example of how structured products can move RWAs beyond simple tokenized ownership. The same model could eventually support tailored payoffs across equities, commodities, and other onchain assets.
